title: Stabilize hourly anchoring to prevent invoice wobble from late-usage arrivals
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: We frequently observe small, non-deterministic adjustments on customer invoices after late usage events land (webhooks / backfill pipelines). These adjustments manifest as one-off negative or positive lines and cause partner confusion + reconciliation churn for finance. Hypothesis: the root cause is inconsistent hourly anchoring of late usage when rate-limit credits and burst credits are applied across overlapping invoice boundaries, combined with nondeterministic ordering in the export job (hour bucketing + rounding).

Impact: Affects invoiced customers receiving burst credits/rate-limit credits; generates mid-cycle invoice noise and manual overrides. Finance has flagged ~12 accounts in Feb with >$1k cumulative adjustments. Our SLA for invoice stability is affected for billed customers on reserved capacity.

Goal: Ensure deterministic, idempotent invoice line generation for late-arriving usage that guarantees stable anchors (hour -> invoice line mapping) and deterministic rounding so that repeated replays or reordered inputs do not change exported invoice lines.

Scope: Billing export / reconciler that writes Stripe line items and NetSuite CSVs; the hourly bucketing code path and the late-usage backfill window. Does NOT include UI billing presentation or downstream ledger reprocessing (separate follow-up).

Proposed solution summary:
1) Define an explicit anchoring rule: late usage is anchored to the invoice period by invoice boundary + source timestamp, and bucketed into fixed hourly slots aligned to UTC hour boundaries. For usage with arrival_timestamp > invoice_close_time, apply a "deferred bucket" tag, but do not retroactively shift existing invoice anchors.
2) Make rounding deterministic: adopt banker's rounding at per-customer aggregation boundary, and emit an export-level checksum (sha256) of the sorted line-item tuples to detect nondeterminism.
3) Enforce deterministic ordering in reconciler exports: sort usage events by (customer_id, anchored_hour, usage_id) before aggregation to prevent variance across replays.
4) Apply a one-time migration where we re-run reconciliation for invoices in the affected window (2026-01-15..2026-02-28) with the new anchoring rules in a sandbox and compare diffs before any live re-emit.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for new anchoring logic and rounding rules.
- Integration test that replays synthetic late-arrival streams in both random and sorted arrival orders; export hashes must match.
- Staging reconciliation run against a snapshot of the billing DB that contains known problematic customers.
- Canary rerun for 50 live accounts for 48h with export-anomaly detection enabled.

Rollout plan:
- Merge changes behind feature flag (billing.deterministic_anchoring).
- Run migration in sandbox, publish diff report to finance and billing-ops.
- Enable for small canary cohort (50 accounts) for 48h. If green, enable for 10% then 100% of accounts over 72h with monitoring.

Acceptance criteria: (see acceptance_criteria field)

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Rounding strategy: banker's rounding reduces aggregate drift but may change a tiny fraction of historical invoices if we re-emit. Finance prefers no historical mutation; therefore we will not re-emit retroactively unless diffs are material and authorized.
- Legacy exporters: NetSuite CSV template expects stable ordering; ensure our added checksum and new deterministic ordering are backward-compatible.
- Performance: sorting large backfill windows could increase memory usage. Plan to implement streaming external sort for >1M events per customer-day.

Links: see links field for initial artifacts and the prototype PR.
acceptance_criteria: Deterministic export hash is identical across 100 randomized replays of the same input set
No invoice line changes observed in canary cohort for non-backfill events
Finance approves diff report for sandbox run (diffs documented and justified)
Metrics: export_anomaly_rate < 0.1% in canary and subsequent rollouts
